note.title: The First Blue
note.text: About 6,000 years ago, at Huaca Prieta on the coast of Peru, people dyed cotton with indigo from a plant and wove it into blue-striped cloth. Scraps of it lay buried in a great mound of earth and stone until archaeologists dug them up. In 2016 chemists found the indigo in their threads: the oldest indigo-dyed cloth known, about 1,600 years older than any found in Egypt. Long before any loom read a pattern, weavers had paint to weave with.

note.title: Artificial Lapis
note.text: In ancient Egypt the finest blue was lapis lazuli, a rare and costly stone. By about 3250 BC Egyptian craftsmen had learned to make a blue of their own, by heating sand, lime and copper together in a furnace. They called it artificial lapis lazuli, and it is the oldest paint known to be made rather than dug from the ground. For thousands of years it painted walls, statues and pots: a rare blue, made plentiful.

note.title: A Loom That Kept Its Pattern
note.text: In 2013 archaeologists in Chengdu, China, opened a tomb from the second century BC and found four wooden models of looms, a sixth of full size, with little painted weavers beside them. Each loom kept its pattern in a row of shafts, and every shaft lifted the threads of one row of the pattern. Lifting the shafts in turn, again and again, wove the pattern over and over. They are the oldest models of pattern looms known anywhere.

note.title: The Paper Strip
note.text: In the silk town of Lyon, weaving a pattern was slow: before every pass of the shuttle, a helper had to pull the cords of the right threads by hand. In 1725 Basile Bouchon, whose father built organs, gave the loom a long strip of paper punched with holes instead. The holes chose which threads would lift, one row of holes for each row of cloth. For the first time, a loom read its picture from paper.

note.title: Jacquard's Loom
note.text: Joseph-Marie Jacquard, a Lyon weaver's son, built his loom out of what others had found. In Paris he studied a loom by Jacques de Vaucanson, the maker of a famous mechanical duck, and joined its ideas to Falcon's chain of cards. His loom of 1804 let one weaver weave the richest pattern with no helper at the cords. By 1812 some 11,000 of them were working in France.

note.title: The Woven Portrait
note.text: In 1839 a Lyon workshop wove a portrait of Jacquard on one of his own looms, from some 24,000 cards. It was silk in black, white and every grey between, and so fine that two members of London's Royal Academy took it for an engraving. Charles Babbage, who was designing a calculating machine that would read cards, hung a copy in his home and showed it to his visitors.

note.title: Weaving Patterns of Numbers
note.text: In 1843 Ada Lovelace wrote about Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, a machine he had designed to follow punched cards as Jacquard's loom does. "The Analytical Engine weaves … patterns," she wrote, "just as the Jacquard-loom weaves flowers and leaves." She saw that it could work on more than numbers: given the rules of music, it might even compose. The engine was never built, but her notes are still read today.
